section.title: The Priests of Nob Killed
section.sectionRationale: Saul's spiral into paranoid violence reaches its horror here: at his command Doeg the Edomite slaughters the priests of the LORD at Nob, eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod, because Saul's own soldiers will not lift a hand against the LORD's priests. Only Ahimelech's son Abiathar escapes, fleeing to the cave-dwelling David, who has already begun gathering the distressed, indebted, and discontented of Israel. The chapter sets the murderous rejected king against the sheltering anointed king in the sharpest possible contrast.
section.thesis: While Saul's men refuse to touch the priests of the LORD, Doeg the Edomite massacres Nob at Saul's naked command, and only Abiathar escapes; David, himself a hunted fugitive, gathers society's castoffs at Adullam and takes personal responsibility for the one priest left alive, a shadow of the true Shepherd-King who gathers the weary and loses none the Father has given Him.
section.frameNote: Five scenes: David gathers a company of the distressed at Adullam and Mizpeh; Saul's paranoid accusation and Doeg's report about Ahimelech; Ahimelech's honest defense before the king; Saul's massacre of the priests of Nob after his own soldiers refuse; and Abiathar's escape to David with the ephod.

units.label: David Gathers at Adullam and Mizpeh

verses.text: So David left Gath and took refuge in the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and the rest of his father's household heard about it, they went down to him there.
And all who were distressed or indebted or discontented rallied around him, and he became their leader. About four hundred men were with him.
From there David went to Mizpeh of Moab, where he said to the king of Moab, “Please let my father and mother stay with you until I learn what God will do for me.”
So he left them in the care of the king of Moab, and they stayed with him the whole time David was in the stronghold.
Then the prophet Gad said to David, “Do not stay in the stronghold. Depart and go into the land of Judah.” So David left and went to the forest of Hereth.

Soon Saul learned that David and his men had been discovered. At that time Saul was sitting under the tamarisk tree on the hill at Gibeah, with his spear in hand and all his servants standing around him.
Then Saul said to his servants, “Listen, men of Benjamin! Is the son of Jesse giving all of you fields and vineyards and making you commanders of thousands or hundreds?

Is that why all of you have conspired against me? Not one of you told me that my own son had made a covenant with the son of Jesse. Not one of you has shown concern for me or revealed to me that my son has stirred up my own servant to lie in wait against me, as is the case today.”
But Doeg the Edomite, who had stationed himself with Saul's servants, answered: “I saw the son of Jesse come to Ahimelech son of Ahitub at Nob.
Ahimelech inquired of the LORD for him and gave him provisions. He also gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.”
Then the king sent messengers to summon Ahimelech the {{kohen|priest}}, the son of Ahitub, and his father's whole family, who were priests at Nob. And all of them came to the king.
“Listen now, son of Ahitub,” said Saul. “Here I am, my lord,” he replied.

And Saul asked him, “Why have you and the son of Jesse conspired against me? You gave him bread and a sword and inquired of God for him so that he could rise up against me to lie in wait, as he is doing today.”
Ahimelech answered the king, “Who among all your servants is as faithful as David, the king's son-in-law, the captain of your bodyguard and honored in your house?

Was that day the first time I inquired of God for him? Far be it from me! Let not the king accuse your servant or any of my father's household, for your servant knew nothing of this whole affair, not in part or in whole.”
But the king replied, “You will surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father's house!”

units.label: The Priests of Nob Slaughtered
units.note: the king's servants would not lift a hand

verses.text: Then the king ordered the guards at his side, “Turn and kill the priests of the LORD, because they too sided with David. For they knew he was fleeing, but they did not tell me.” But the king's servants would not lift a hand to strike the priests of the LORD.

So the king ordered Doeg, “You turn and strike down the priests!” And Doeg the Edomite turned and struck down the priests himself. On that day he killed eighty-five men who wore the linen {{ephod|ephod}}.
He also put to the sword Nob, the city of the priests, with its men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys, and sheep.

units.label: Abiathar Escapes to David with the Ephod
units.note: he who seeks your life is seeking mine

verses.text: But one of the sons of Ahimelech son of Ahitub escaped. His name was Abiathar, and he fled to David.
And Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the LORD.
Then David said to Abiathar, “I knew that Doeg the Edomite was there that day, and that he was sure to tell Saul. I myself am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father's house.
Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks your {{nephesh|life}} is seeking mine as well. You will be safe with me.”

kohen.gloss: Priest. Ahimelech the kohen and his household serve at Nob; Saul's order to kill the LORD's kohanim, refused by his own soldiers, verse 17, shows how far the rejected king has fallen, willing to slaughter God's own consecrated servants.

ephod.gloss: A priestly garment worn by those who served before the LORD. Verse 18 marks the eighty-five slain as priests in active office, and Abiathar carries an ephod to David, 1 Samuel 23:6, preserving Israel's God-given means of inquiring of the LORD through the disaster.

nephesh.gloss: Soul, life, the whole self. In verse 23 David says he who seeks your nephesh is seeking mine as well, binding Abiathar's fate to his own, a picture of a shepherd-king who shares the danger of those he shelters rather than standing at a safe distance.

basic.context: David is now a fugitive with nothing: he has just faked madness to escape Gath, and here he takes refuge in a cave at Adullam. Slowly a small army forms around him, not warriors of renown but people in trouble, the distressed, the indebted, the discontented. Meanwhile at Saul's court, the king's paranoia curdles into open cruelty. He learns, through the spy Doeg, that the priest Ahimelech helped David at Nob, gave him bread and Goliath's sword, and inquired of the LORD for him. Saul summons the whole priestly family and, when his own soldiers refuse to kill God's priests, orders Doeg to do it himself. Eighty-five priests and the entire town of Nob, men, women, children, even livestock, are slaughtered. Only one son, Abiathar, escapes to David with the priestly ephod. The chapter asks a stark question: who is the true king, the one who murders the LORD's priests, or the one who shelters the LORD's broken people?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, not a manual to imitate. Saul's massacre is condemned by the narrative itself, most pointedly by his own soldiers' refusal to obey and by David's grief and sense of guilt. The chapter describes the depths to which Saul's rejection of the LORD carries him, and it describes David's response of taking responsibility, not as a command to copy in every detail but as a picture of righteous, shepherding leadership.
basic.originalLanguages: Ahimelech is called kohen, priest, marking exactly who Saul is willing to destroy, the LORD's own consecrated servants. The eighty-five slain wore the linen ephod, the garment of priestly office, so the text underlines that this was a massacre of worshippers, not merely political rivals. And David, taking in the sole survivor, says he who seeks your nephesh, your very life, is seeking mine as well, binding his own fate to the man he now shelters.
basic.typology: David gathering the distressed, indebted, and discontented under his wing while himself a hunted man foreshadows Christ, who invites the weary and burdened, and who said of those the Father gave Him, I have lost none. Abiathar's rescue by the true, though not yet enthroned, king pictures how those fleeing judgment find safety only with the anointed one, not with the reigning power that has turned against God.
basic.christ: Saul, the rejected king, murders the LORD's own priests when they will not betray the anointed one; David, the anointed but not yet enthroned king, gathers the broken and takes on himself responsibility for the danger surrounding Abiathar. This is a small but real foreshadowing of Jesus, the true King who came to those weary and burdened, and who declared of His own, I have lost none of those You have given Me. Where earthly power kills the innocent to protect itself, the true King absorbs the danger and offers shelter.
basic.god: God does not prevent this atrocity, yet He is not absent, the priesthood at Nob is not annihilated, one survives to carry both the ephod, the means of inquiring of the LORD, and the line, to David. God preserves a remnant even through unthinkable violence, and He is already moving history toward the throne He has promised David, using even Saul's crimes to drive the priesthood toward the rightful king.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Samuel 2 records the earlier judgment on Eli's priestly house, of which this massacre is a grim fulfillment. Psalm 52 is David's reflection on Doeg's treachery. Matthew 11 gives Christ's invitation to the weary. John 6 and John 18 show Christ losing none the Father has given Him.
basic.oneStory: Saul's rejection of the LORD collapses into the murder of His own priests, while the fugitive David, already living as a true though hidden king, shelters the one survivor and every broken soul who comes to him. This scene sharpens the contrast the whole book is building between the king Israel chose and the king God is raising up, and it points ahead to the greater Son of David who gathers the lost and guards them to the end.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as a diptych, David's camp forming in verses one through five, then Saul's court unraveling in verses six through twenty three, and the two panels are joined by a single, damning contrast: David gathers refugees no one else wanted, while Saul, surrounded by his own tribesmen and his spear always in hand, verse six, cannot gather even minimal loyalty, since his own servants withhold from him exactly the information he most wants.

Saul's speech in verses seven and eight is a small masterpiece of paranoid rhetoric, framed entirely around what David has supposedly given the Benjamites, fields, vineyards, commands, none of which the narrative has shown David distributing to anyone. The accusation reveals more about Saul's fears than about any actual conspiracy, and it sets up Doeg's damaging testimony as the answer to a question built on false premises.

The massacre scene escalates in three deliberate stages: the king's own guards refuse outright, verse seventeen, forcing Saul to repeat the order to Doeg alone, verse eighteen, and then the violence spreads from the eighty five priests themselves to the entire town, its women, children, infants, and even its livestock, verse nineteen, a totalizing destruction usually reserved in Scripture for Israel's enemies, now turned by an Israelite king against Israel's own priesthood. The final scene compresses grief into four short verses, Abiathar's flight, his report, and David's immediate, unflinching acceptance of responsibility, closing the chapter not with vengeance but with shelter offered.
context.historical:
Adullam's cave sat in the Judean foothills near the border of Philistine territory, a natural refuge riddled with defensible hiding places, and its location explains why David's extended family, vulnerable to Saul's reach at their home in Bethlehem, could relocate there quickly once word spread. The distressed, indebted, and discontented who join him, verse two, describe a recognizable social class in the ancient Near East, people crushed by debt, dispossessed farmers, and those alienated from a court that favored Saul's own tribe; David's band begins not as an army of heroes but as a company of Israel's economic and social casualties.

Sending his parents to the king of Moab, verse three, likely traded on David's own great grandmother Ruth being a Moabite; a family connection to Moabite lineage would explain why David expected a foreign king to shelter his aging parents rather than exploit their vulnerability.

Doeg's identity as an Edomite matters historically. Edom and Israel had a long history of hostility going back to Esau and Jacob, and a foreign herdsman serving in Saul's court, however trusted, would have felt none of the native Israelite scruple against striking down the LORD's own priests. Ancient readers would have recognized the irony immediately, an outsider does what covenant kinship should have made unthinkable for any of Saul's own countrymen, exposing exactly how far outside Israel's own values Saul's court had drifted under his declining reign.
context.canonical:
This chapter functions as the grim hinge between two priesthoods. The oracle against Eli's house, I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest, 1 Samuel 2:35, is answered here in the harshest possible way, not by Eli's own line simply fading, but by an entire priestly community put to the sword in a single day, so that only Abiathar, carrying the ephod, survives to reach the man that same oracle was quietly pointing toward all along.

Psalm 52 gives the episode its own prophetic commentary from David's pen, addressing Doeg's treachery in its heading and contrasting the boastful, sword tongued mighty man who trusts in wealth with the righteous who flourish like a green olive tree in the house of God, Psalm 52:7-8, a direct theological verdict on the very man who slaughtered Nob.

The chapter's forward reach extends across the rest of David's life. Abiathar becomes David's lifelong priest and adviser, present at Ziklag, 1 Samuel 30:7, and through the years of David's reign, until Solomon finally deposes him for supporting Adonijah's rival claim to the throne, fulfilling in slow motion the same word spoken against Eli's house generations earlier, 1 Kings 2:26-27. What begins as a single day of horror at Nob threads all the way through Israel's history into the establishment of Solomon's kingdom.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants a reader who has followed Saul from chapter thirteen's impatient sacrifice, through chapter fifteen's disobedience over Amalek, to see the full trajectory that pattern was always heading toward: a king so consumed by suspicion that he will order, and eventually accept from a foreigner's hand, the murder of God's own consecrated servants. Nothing in the earlier chapters directly predicts a massacre, yet the writer structures Saul's decline so that this atrocity reads as the logical, horrifying endpoint of small compromises left unaddressed.

At the same moment, the writer wants readers to notice what true kingship actually looks like in embryo. David, with no crown, no palace, and no legal authority of any kind, nonetheless takes personal responsibility for a stranger's safety, naming his own conscience as the reason Abiathar must be sheltered rather than merely pitied. The juxtaposition is deliberate: Israel already has a king who kills his own priesthood to protect his position, and Israel already has, hidden in a cave, the king who will protect his people even at cost to himself.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Saul's order and Doeg's obedience are recorded, never commanded; the narrative condemns the massacre by every means available to Hebrew storytelling short of an explicit editorial statement, showing the king's own soldiers refusing the order and letting a foreigner do what no Israelite would touch. No reader is meant to conclude that religious or political authority may ever justify violence against those who serve God faithfully.

David's self-accusation in verse twenty two is the description of one man's tender, perhaps overly severe, conscience rather than a legal ruling on causation; Scripture elsewhere places the guilt for innocent blood squarely on the one who sheds it, not merely on someone whose earlier choices formed part of the chain of events. What transfers to believers is the underlying instinct behind David's words, a willingness to feel the weight of harm connected to our own actions rather than deflecting all responsibility onto others, paired with practical, costly care for those who suffer because of it.

debates.question: Is David morally responsible for the deaths at Nob?

views.label: David bears real, if indirect, guilt
views.case: David himself says, in effect, I am responsible for the lives of your father's house, verse 22, and he had not warned Ahimelech that Doeg witnessed their meeting in chapter 21; his own words show a conscience troubled by the connection between his flight and their deaths.

views.label: Saul alone bears the moral guilt of murder
views.case: Ahimelech acted in innocent ignorance, verse 15, and it is Saul who orders the massacre and Doeg who carries it out; David deceived Ahimelech about his situation in chapter 21, but he did not command or desire the priests' deaths.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree David feels and accepts responsibility without excusing Saul's crime; the tension teaches that even innocent involvement in another's suffering can rightly weigh on a conscience, while ultimate blame still rests with the one who gives the murderous order.

debates.question: Why would Saul's own soldiers refuse a direct royal command?

views.label: Reverence for the LORD's priests overrode loyalty to the king
views.case: Even soldiers serving an increasingly erratic Saul recognized that raising a hand against consecrated priests of the LORD crossed a line no command could justify.

views.label: Political self-preservation
views.case: Killing the priesthood risked wider outrage and divine judgment on the whole army, so refusal may have been as much prudence as piety.

debates.bearing: Either way, the refusal exposes how isolated Saul has become, not even his own men will follow him into this atrocity, and only a foreign mercenary will.

study.originalLanguages:
Saul's accusation to his own tribesmen turns on a single loaded word, qesher, conspired, verses eight and thirteen. This is the vocabulary of political treason throughout the historical books, used later for the palace coups that topple kings, 2 Kings 11:14, 15:10; by reaching for this term against men who have done nothing but stay silent, Saul reveals that in his mind mere silence has become indistinguishable from armed rebellion.

Ahimelech's defense turns on an equally loaded word. He calls David faithful, more faithful than any other servant in Saul's house, verse fourteen, the Hebrew ne'eman, using the identical root behind the LORD's own promise concerning Eli's replacement, I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest, 1 Samuel 2:35. The irony is exact and devastating: the priest who calls David faithful, using the very word attached to the coming faithful priest, will himself be killed within the hour, while the promise his own words unconsciously echo continues moving toward its fulfillment in someone else entirely.

Saul's death sentence against you and all your father's house, verse sixteen, deliberately recycles the language of the earlier oracle against Eli, that the LORD would cut off the strength of your father's house, 1 Samuel 2:31, 33. Saul, without realizing it, becomes the instrument carrying out judgment language first spoken against this very family generations before, so that his personal cruelty and God's announced justice arrive at the same address by entirely different roads.

Finally, sword threads through both this chapter and the one before it. Goliath's sword, taken from Nob in chapter twenty one, gave David a weapon of past deliverance; here Saul commands that the priests be put to the sword, and the same word describes Nob itself being struck down to the sword, verse nineteen. The single recurring word marks the tragic reversal running through these two chapters, an instrument of rescue for God's anointed becomes an instrument of slaughter against God's own servants. Even the guards' refusal, they would not lift a hand, anticipates the identical idiom David himself will use of Saul in the chapters that follow, may I never lift my hand against him, 1 Samuel 24:6, 10, so that Saul's own soldiers here model, without praise or comment from the narrator, the very restraint David will later have to explain and defend at length before Saul's face.

typology.type: David gathering the distressed, indebted, and discontented at Adullam
typology.fulfillment: David's growing company of debtors, the distressed, and the discontented anticipates Christ's own gathering of society's rejected, tax collectors, sinners, and the sick who need a physician rather than the healthy who claim they do not, Mark 2:17, Luke 15:1-2. The correspondence is real, both kings assemble a following from exactly the people established power has discarded, yet the escalation is total: David could offer only a fugitive's shared danger, while Christ offers rest for the weary and burdened, Matthew 11:28-30, and transforms society's outcasts not into a private militia but into citizens of an everlasting kingdom.

typology.type: David taking personal responsibility for endangered Abiathar
typology.fulfillment: David's blunt admission, I am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father's house, verse twenty two, is a fugitive's guilty conscience rather than a legal rescue, since he can offer Abiathar nothing but shared danger in a cave. Christ's declaration that He loses none the Father has given Him, John 6:39, and that He lays down His life so His sheep may live, John 10:11, 15, escalates this pattern from mere acceptance of blame into active, willing substitution, the good shepherd actually absorbing the wolf's attack rather than merely regretting that it happened.

typology.type: Abiathar escaping to the rejected but rightful king with the ephod
typology.fulfillment: Access to God through the ephod's sacred lots survives the disaster at Nob only because one priest reaches the rejected but rightful king; every other channel to inquire of the LORD in Israel has just been destroyed. This anticipates how access to God after the collapse of every human priesthood survives only through the one true and rightful King, our great high priest who has passed through the heavens, able to sympathize with our weakness and to be approached with confidence, Hebrews 4:14-16.

study.christ:
Saul ends this chapter as the very opposite of what a shepherd king should be, ordering the death of the men who serve at God's altar because they will not betray his rival. The horror is compounded by whose hand finally strikes: not an Israelite at all, but Doeg the Edomite, an outsider willing to do what covenant loyalty made unthinkable for Saul's own countrymen. Israel's anointed king has become, in this one act, less faithful to the LORD than a foreign mercenary is loyal to him.

Against that backdrop, David's response reads as an early, imperfect sketch of the true King still centuries away. He gathers exactly the people no one else wanted, he receives news of catastrophic loss without deflecting blame, and he offers shelter to the one survivor at cost to his own already precarious safety, stay with me, do not be afraid, verse twenty three. Every one of these gestures anticipates something Christ will do completely rather than partially: where David could only share danger, Christ absorbs it outright, declaring that whoever comes to Him He will never cast out, John 6:37, and that no one will snatch His sheep out of His hand, John 10:28.

The contrast with Saul sharpens the picture further. Saul kills the priesthood to protect his own throne; Christ, our great high priest, offers His own body so that others might live, becoming both the sacrifice and the one who intercedes, Hebrews 7:25, 9:14. Where Saul's guards refused a wicked order and only a foreigner complied, every disciple of Jesus is called to refuse the world's demand to abandon those Christ has gathered, following instead the pattern of a King who took on Himself exactly the danger meant for His people, he who seeks their life sought His own first, and laid it down willingly, John 10:17-18.

Even the detail of the ephod matters typologically. It travels from a doomed priesthood to a hunted king, preserving Israel's access to divine guidance through the very worst catastrophe imaginable, a small but real anticipation of how the way to God, torn open at the cross rather than closed by human violence, survives every collapse of merely human religious institutions, Hebrews 10:19-20.
study.god:
The God of this chapter holds together two things that never separate cleanly for very long: righteous judgment already spoken and mercy still quietly at work. Long before Saul was ever crowned, the LORD had announced that the strength of Eli's house would be cut off and its members would die by the sword, 1 Samuel 2:31, 33. This chapter is that word coming true, but through an agent, Saul's own paranoid cruelty, that nobody would have named as God's chosen instrument. God does not manufacture Saul's sin to accomplish His purposes, yet He does not let Saul's sin escape His purposes either; both truths sit side by side without the narrator feeling any need to resolve the tension for the reader.

At the very moment total loss seems certain, eighty five priests, a whole town, every visible sign of the sanctuary's continuity, God preserves exactly one thread: Abiathar, and with him the ephod. This is not a dramatic miracle; it is one young man running fast enough and far enough to reach the right person. God's providence in this chapter, as in the one before it, operates through timing and human choices rather than through visible interruption of the ordinary. Israel's access to God, hanging by a single life, is never actually lost, because the LORD had already determined where that single life would land.

The chapter is also honest that God does not spare the innocent from every consequence of another's sin. Eighty five men die, and an entire town's population and livestock with them; nothing softens that horror or explains it away. What the chapter offers instead is the assurance that God's justice and covenant purposes keep moving even through catastrophe, so that neither Saul's violence nor the world's worst days can finally overturn what God has determined to do.

Nothing here asks a reader to admire Saul's outcome or to treat Nob's dead as an acceptable cost. The narrator lets the horror stand in full, and lets Doeg's obedience stand in stark, deliberate contrast to the refusal of Saul's own soldiers, precisely so that God's ultimate governance over this history is never mistaken for approval of the means by which Saul pursued his own security.

crossReferences.note: A man of God warns Eli that his house's strength will be cut off and that a faithful priest will be raised up in its place; this chapter is that first half of the warning fulfilled in the most brutal way imaginable, while Abiathar's escape quietly keeps the second half of the promise moving forward.

The LORD's promise to raise up a faithful priest for Himself supplies the very word, faithful, that Ahimelech ironically applies to David just before his own death, tying this massacre directly to a promise spoken a generation earlier.

David's own reflection on Doeg's treachery, naming him directly and contrasting his boastful violence with the psalmist's trust in God's steadfast love, the closest thing Scripture gives to David's private response to this chapter's horror.

Solomon finally removes Abiathar from the priesthood for backing a rival claim to the throne, completing in slow motion the judgment against Eli's house that the massacre at Nob had already carried out in blood.

Christ's invitation to the weary and burdened matches, and infinitely exceeds, David's gathering of the distressed, indebted, and discontented at Adullam, both kings drawing society's casualties toward themselves rather than away.

Jesus promises that He will never cast out anyone who comes to Him and that He loses none the Father has given Him, the pattern David dimly reflects when he draws the sole survivor of Nob under his own protection.

The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep rather than fleeing like a hired hand who does not truly own them, the standard David's costly, if limited, care for Abiathar begins to gesture toward.

Believers are urged to approach the throne of grace with confidence because of a great high priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses, the ultimate answer to a chapter where Israel's earthly high priesthood is nearly wiped out in a single afternoon.

The visit to Nob that this chapter's massacre punishes; reading the two chapters together shows exactly how David's request for bread and a sword becomes, through Doeg's silent watching, the unintended cause of an entire town's destruction.

study.oneStory:
This chapter sits deep inside the long story of Israel demanding a king like the nations, receiving Saul, and watching that choice curdle into exactly the abuse Samuel warned would come, 1 Samuel 8:11-18. Here the warning arrives in its most extreme form: a king who takes not fields and sons but the very lives of the LORD's own priests, revealing that human kingship, left to itself, always eventually turns its power against the people and institutions meant to serve God.

Yet the chapter refuses to end there. In the same movement that records Saul's worst atrocity, it shows the true king already functioning as a true king long before his coronation, gathering the broken, taking on responsibility for danger not his own, and preserving, almost by accident, the one surviving link to Israel's access to God. The contrast is the engine driving the entire second half of 1 Samuel forward: which king will Israel actually get, the one crowned by human choice or the one anointed by God and now hiding in a cave.

Read across the whole Bible, Nob's destruction and Adullam's gathering rehearse, on a small scale, a pattern that recurs whenever earthly power turns violent against God's people, judgment for the guilty, and shelter under the coming king for those the world has cast aside. The story does not resolve here; it moves forward instead toward the greater Son of David, who will one day gather every nation's distressed and discontented into an everlasting kingdom, absorb every danger meant for His people rather than merely sharing it, and stand, at the very end, as both the perfect priest that Nob's priesthood only imperfectly pictured and the perfect King that neither Saul nor David, in the end, ever fully was.

quiz.q: Why did Saul's own guards refuse to carry out his order to kill the priests of Nob?

options.text: They would not lift a hand against the priests of the LORD, even at the king's command.
options.note: Verse 17 states plainly that the king's servants would not strike the priests of the LORD.

options.text: They feared national outrage if the priesthood were harmed.
options.note: A plausible motive, but the text names their reason simply as refusing to strike the LORD's priests, not political calculation.

options.text: They doubted Ahimelech was actually guilty of conspiracy.
options.note: The text does not say they judged the case; it simply records their refusal to touch the priests.

options.text: They agreed with Saul but were too slow to act before Doeg intervened.
options.note: The text says they would not lift a hand at all, not that they were merely slow.

quiz.q: What did Doeg the Edomite do at Saul's command?

options.text: He struck down eighty-five priests who wore the linen ephod and put the city of Nob to the sword.
options.note: Verses 18-19 record this in full detail, including women, children, and livestock.

options.text: He killed Ahimelech alone as the responsible party.
options.note: Doeg did far more than kill one man; the massacre extended to the whole priestly family and the town.

options.text: He reported Ahimelech's aid to David but refused to raise a hand himself.
options.note: Doeg's report in verses 9-10 led to this, but he also personally carried out the killing in verses 18-19.

options.text: He refused Saul's order along with the other soldiers.
options.note: The opposite is true; Doeg alone obeyed and carried out the massacre.

quiz.q: Who escaped the massacre at Nob, and where did he go?

options.text: Abiathar, a son of Ahimelech, escaped and fled to David with the ephod.
options.note: Verse 20 records his escape, and 1 Samuel 23:6 records his bringing the ephod to David.

options.text: Ahimelech himself escaped to Gibeah.
options.note: Ahimelech was killed with the rest of the priests; it was his son Abiathar who escaped, and not to Gibeah but to David.

options.text: Several priests escaped into the wilderness of Judah.
options.note: Only Abiathar is named as escaping; the text does not mention other survivors.

options.text: No one survived the massacre.
options.note: Abiathar survived and reached David; the priestly line was not entirely cut off.

quiz.q: How did David respond when Abiathar reached him?

options.text: He took responsibility, saying the one who sought Abiathar's life sought his own, and offered him shelter.
options.note: Verses 22-23 show David naming his own role and promising safety.

options.text: He immediately marched to avenge the priests on Saul.
options.note: David expresses grief and responsibility, but the text does not record an immediate military reprisal here.

options.text: He sent Abiathar away to protect his own men from Saul's wrath.
options.note: David does the opposite, he draws Abiathar in and promises him safety with him.

options.text: He blamed Abiathar for bringing trouble upon him.
options.note: David blames himself, not Abiathar, for what happened.

quiz.q: How does this chapter point toward Christ?

options.text: David, a hunted king, shelters the broken and takes responsibility for those endangered because of him, foreshadowing Christ who gathers the weary and loses none the Father gives Him.
options.note: This is the heart of the typology, echoed in John 6:37-39, 18:9, and Matthew 11:28.

options.text: It shows that God always protects His people from every harm in this life.
options.note: The chapter shows God preserving a remnant and a purpose, not a promise of immunity from all suffering; eighty-five priests and a town did perish.

options.text: It teaches mainly that political power always corrupts absolutely.
options.note: True of Saul here, but the chapter's center is the contrast with David's shepherding response, not a general political lesson.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament.
options.note: The contrast between the murderous rejected king and the sheltering anointed king points directly toward Christ.

questions: Saul's own men would not touch the LORD's priests, yet Doeg did. What does this scene teach you about the danger of surrounding yourself with people willing to do anything you ask, right or wrong?
David said, I am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father's house. Where might your choices be putting others at risk in ways you have not yet owned?
Abiathar lost everything, his father, his family, his home, in a single day. How do you process grief and loss that comes through no fault of your own?

David gathered the distressed, indebted, and discontented, the outcasts of Israel, around himself before he ever wore a crown. Who around you might need the kind of shelter David offered, and are you willing to offer it before you feel qualified?

Jesus said He loses none the Father has given Him. How does knowing Christ takes responsibility for His people's safety, even at cost to Himself, change how you face days when you feel hunted or unsafe?

translationNotes.note: The BSB reading stay with you follows the Syriac and Vulgate; the Hebrew as preserved reads go forth, noted in the chapter's footnote, a minor variant that does not affect the storyline.
Eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod identifies the slain specifically as priests in active service, not merely townsfolk; the ephod was the distinguishing garment of priestly office.
Abiathar's escape preserves the Aaronic priestly line through Ithamar and sets up his long service to David, continuing until Solomon removes him in 1 Kings 2:26-27.
